segments: Chronography of Barhebraeus.
[578] was alive:
Frankish envoys were continually pressing and coming to him from the Pope of Rome and from other kings,
so that the Mongols should be shoulder-to-shoulder with the Franks,
and they should march against the Egyptians and Pharaoh-like ones, who had grown fat and kicked, and were destroying the Christians and their cities.
And likewise Arghun himself sent as an envoy to the Pope Rabban Bar Sauma, the Uighur monk who had come with the Catholicos Mar Yahballaha from the lands of the Great Khan;
and he confirmed with the Pope covenants and ratifications,
that they should go forth together and destroy the realm of the Arabs {Tayyaye}—
which happened contrary to their intentions.
Now Gaykhatu, when he returned from the lands of the Romans to the mountains of Greater Armenia,
the sons of the kings and the nobles of the Mongols gathered together again,
and took him and seated him upon the throne of the kingdom on the twenty-ninth
of Hazīrān in the year one thousand six hundred and three of the Greeks (1292 of our Lord?).
Now the Egyptians, when they heard that Arghun had recently ended his life,
gathered armies, tens of thousands of people and nations whose number could not be counted,
and went and encamped against Acre, the great and renowned city of the Franks,
which is on the shores of the Great Sea;
and they fought against it a fierce battle for the space of two months.
The Franks within, however, by reason of their pride and their boastfulness,
did not deign to close the gates of the city against them at all,
neither by night nor by day.
And valiantly the Frankish horsemen would sally forth from within,
and cut down as with scythes the Arabs who were outside.
And it is said
that more than twenty thousand human beings from among the Arabs were killed at Acre.
And handsomely and very watchfully they held the city,
until their governor, the great Count, was struck by an arrow and died.
Then those within grew slack,
and those outside were greatly strengthened.
Against that lower wall, which is on the land side, about three hundred mangonels were stationed,
and beneath each tower {pyrgos} about a thousand miners (sappers?){OCR?} who burrow into the ground were crowded,
and they threw down from the wall a tower and two.
Then the wretched brothers and the rest of the nobles began to enter into the fortified courtyards and fight.
